Subordinationism (Error)
sub-or-di-NAY-shun-iz-um
noun (Trinitarian error)
The Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status — making the Son a lesser or derived deity rather than co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. Distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (which involve order but not inequality). Arianism is the extreme form.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and the Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status, making the Son a lesser or derived deity rather than co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. Subordinationism comes in degrees. The extreme form is Arianism (4th century), which held that the Son is a created being, the first and highest of creatures, of a different substance from the Father (heteroousios or at most homoiousios, of like substance, but not homoousios, of the same substance); the Son had a beginning (there was when he was not), is not eternal, and is not fully God. Arianism was condemned at the Council of Nicaea (325), which affirmed the Son homoousios (of one substance) with the Father, eternally begotten, very God of very God. Milder forms of subordinationism stop short of making the Son a creature but still subordinate the Son to the Father in some respect of essence, glory, or authority. The orthodox doctrine must be carefully distinguished from subordinationism. The orthodox Nicene doctrine affirms an order (taxis) among the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin (the Father is the unbegotten source; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Spirit eternally proceeds) — an order of relation and origin, but not of essence, being, glory, or status. The three Persons are co-equal and co-eternal, sharing the one undivided divine essence equally; the order of the relations does not imply any inequality. A contemporary debate concerns the eternal functional subordination of the Son (EFS / ERAS), the view (held by some complementarian theologians and contested by others) that the Son is eternally subordinate to the Father in role/function (though equal in essence); critics charge that this risks a form of subordinationism and compromises the equality of the Persons, while proponents distinguish functional from essential subordination. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene doctrine against subordinationism: the Son is co-equal and co-eternal with the Father, of one substance (homoousios), fully God; the eternal relations of origin involve order but not inequality of essence, glory, or status; and the patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the contemporary EFS debate with appropriate care, holding firmly to the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Trinitarian error subordinating the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status, making the Son a lesser/derived deity; extreme form Arianism (condemned at Nicaea, 325); distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (order without inequality); the contemporary EFS debate.

SUBORDINATIONISM (ERROR), n. (Trinitarian error) Subordinates the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status, making the Son a lesser/derived deity rather than co-equal and co-eternal. Extreme form: Arianism (4th c.; the Son a created being, there was when he was not, not homoousios); condemned at Nicaea (325, the Son homoousios, eternally begotten, very God of very God). Milder forms subordinate the Son in some respect of essence, glory, or authority. Distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (an order/taxis grounded in the relations — Father unbegotten, Son begotten, Spirit proceeding — but not inequality of essence). Contemporary debate: eternal functional subordination (EFS/ERAS).

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 10:30 — "I and my Father are one."

Philippians 2:6 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God."

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Subordinationism makes the Son a lesser or derived deity; the extreme form (Arianism) was condemned at Nicaea; it must be distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (order without inequality of essence).

Subordinationism is the Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status. The extreme form, Arianism, made the Son a created being — the first and highest of creatures, but not eternal and not fully God (there was when he was not); this was decisively condemned at the Council of Nicaea (325), which affirmed the Son homoousios (of one substance) with the Father, eternally begotten, very God of very God. The orthodox doctrine must be carefully distinguished from subordinationism. The Nicene faith affirms an order (taxis) among the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin — the Father is the unbegotten fountainhead, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, the Spirit eternally proceeds — but this is an order of relation and origin, not of essence, glory, or status. The three Persons share the one undivided divine essence equally; they are co-equal and co-eternal; the order of the relations implies no inequality (the eternally-begotten Son is not thereby lesser than the Father, any more than a human son shares the same human nature as his father without being a lesser kind of being). A contemporary debate concerns the eternal functional subordination of the Son (EFS / ERAS), held by some complementarian theologians (who argue the Son is eternally subordinate to the Father in role while equal in essence, sometimes appealing to it as a Trinitarian ground for human gender roles) and contested by others (who charge that it risks subordinationism and compromises the equality of the Persons, and that the eternal relations of origin, not an eternal subordination of role, are the proper Nicene grounding). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene doctrine against subordinationism (the Son co-equal and co-eternal, homoousios with the Father), and engages the EFS debate with appropriate care, holding firmly to the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Subordinates the Son to the Father in essence/being/status; extreme form Arianism (condemned at Nicaea, 325, the Son homoousios); distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (order without inequality); the contemporary EFS debate.
